name: BrowserAct
summary: No-code web scraper and browser-automation bots from one prompt, with managed browsers, residential proxies and CAPTCHA solving in one credit pool. Monthly billing costs 20 to 25 percent more than yearly.
best_for: teams that need a reusable web scraper or browser bot without writing selectors, want the browsers, proxies and CAPTCHA handling managed for them, and can commit to yearly billing -- at $13 a month Basic is a cheap way to run a few scheduled bots
skip_if: you will bill month to month (20 to 25 percent more than yearly, not the doubling the struck-through prices suggest), you plan to run proxy-heavy jobs on the Local CLI (one gigabyte of dynamic proxy traffic is 5,000 credits, half of Basic's monthly pool) or to rely on the cloud proxy staying free, which the page says is for a limited time only, or you need a published overage rate before you commit, because the credit-pack price is not on the page
honest_knock: The yearly toggle wears a -20% badge and the crossed-out prices suggest much more, but read what you would actually be charged on 3 October 2026: monthly is $16, $70 and $120, and yearly is $13, $56 and $96, so paying month to month costs roughly 20 to 25 percent more -- not the doubling the struck-through $20, $100 and $200 imply. Those list prices are the discount's anchor, not a rate anyone is currently charged. The free tier is the bigger catch: its card reads 200 signup credits where it read 1,500 on 2 September, about 66 workflow steps at 3 credits a step, while the vendor's own llms.txt still advertises 2,000. And the 'as low as' step rate does not come from these tiers: llms.txt puts a step at about $0.0019, but at Advanced a credit works out to about $0.00096, so a 3-credit step is roughly $0.0029 -- the lower number must belong to a credit pack whose price the page does not show. In our hands-on run of 4 September (historical test data, priced at the meters of that day) the meter was honest at account level (1,500 to 1,174 credits over one build and two runs, reconciling exactly with the history list), but the same Bot cost 21 credits on one run and 27 on the next for identical output, and the task panel briefly reported 0 credits for a run the list priced at 21.

pricing.notes: (prices re-verified 2026-10-03 on browseract.com/pricing, both billing tabs open, and cross-read against browseract.com/llms.txt the same day) A credit-metered subscription with a free tier. Yearly billing: Basic $13/month ($156), Essential $56/month ($672) and Advanced $96/month ($1,152). Monthly billing: Basic $16 a month with $20 struck through, Essential $70 with $100 struck through, Advanced $120 with $200 struck through. Unchanged since 2026-09-13; before that, on 2026-09-02, the public page charged the struck-through list prices on the monthly tab. The Free Trial card reads 200 Free Credits on signup, 2 Free Agent Builds, 2 simultaneous tasks and 5 free local browsers (1,500 on 2026-09-02); the vendor's own llms.txt still says 2,000 free credits, and both llms.txt and BrowserAct in writing name the pricing page as the source of truth, so we quote the card. Paid allowances: 10,000, 50,000 and 100,000 credits a month with 10, 20 and 40 simultaneous tasks, unlimited MCP servers, up to 5, 25 and 50 static proxies, 10, 50 and 100 free local browsers, a 7-day free trial per paid tier (1,000, 1,500 and 2,000 credits) and access to extra credit packs. CHANGED SINCE 2026-09-20: a Workflow Bot step now costs 3 credits instead of 5. The page splits usage in two. Cloud SaaS: Workflow Bots at 3 credits per executed step, Agent Bots estimated at 300-500 credits to build and 10-20 a run for a simple task, 800-1,500 to build and 20-30 a run for a complex one; the 24/7 cloud browser and the built-in dynamic proxy are free for a limited time, and a static proxy is optional. Local CLI: $0 runtime fee; credits apply only to optional add-ons, a local fingerprint browser at 100 credits, dynamic proxy at 5,000 credits per GB, static proxies priced by location and tier without a figure.

compare_with.name: Browse.ai
compare_with.why: Both turn a website into a scheduled, reusable data robot without code. Browse.ai is the older name and prices per robot run on a credit ladder that starts at $19 a month on annual billing, $48 monthly; BrowserAct starts lower at $13 yearly and bundles managed browsers, proxies and CAPTCHA solving into the same credit pool. If your bottleneck is blocked pages, BrowserAct's infrastructure is the difference; if it is simply extracting a table on a schedule, either does the job and Browse.ai has the longer track record.

sessions.what: Historical test data: these are measurements from 4 September 2026, at that day's free allowance and meters, not today's Free plan or the standard cost of every Bot. We ran the reproducible test BrowserAct's own partner team proposed, on a free account with the 1,500 sign-up credits the card offered at the time. The prompt, verbatim: open books.toscrape.com, collect the first 20 books in listing order, open each detail page and return full title, displayed price, availability and source URL, leave unavailable fields blank, infer nothing. Before touching BrowserAct we fetched the same 20 pages with plain HTTP and saved the four fields as ground truth, so every value below was checked against the source, not against BrowserAct's own claims. Then we built the Bot from the prompt, ran it twice from the published version, and read the credit meter after each step.
findings: Accuracy: 80 of 80 fields correct, three times over. The build's own verification output, run 1 and run 2 each returned 20 rows with title, price, availability and URL identical to our ground truth, including the parenthetical stock counts ('In stock (22 available)') and the currency symbol, which the Bot kept as displayed rather than converting.

The build costs more than the runs. Building the Bot took 4 minutes 59 seconds and 278 credits; the agent inspected the listing and a detail page, wrote a small package (a SKILL.md, a run.py and two DOM helpers), compiled it, and ran it end to end before declaring it ready. On that day's free tier that was about a fifth of the sign-up credits spent before the first real run. The pricing page now estimates 300 to 500 credits for a simple Agent build, and today's free card lists 2 free Agent Builds alongside its 200 credits.

Runs are cheap but not deterministic in cost. Run 1 used 21 credits in 1 minute 56 seconds; run 2, the same Bot on the same 20 pages, used 27 credits in 3 minutes 12 seconds. Identical output, 29% more credits and 65% more wall time. At Basic's 10,000 credits for $13 a month on yearly billing, a run of this size is roughly three cents, so the variance is small in money and worth knowing about in budgeting.

The meter is honest at the account level and confusing at the task level. Balance went 1,500 to 1,222 after the build, 1,201 after run 1 and 1,174 after run 2, which reconciles exactly with the per-task figures in the history list. But the task detail panel showed 'Credits used: 0' for a run that the history list, seconds later, priced at 21. Trust the list and the balance, not the panel.

The agent made one silent design decision. The prompt said 'the first 20 books', and the Bot was built with no parameters and 'first 20' hard-coded; it says so in its own summary and offers to change it on request. Fine for this test, but a Bot you intend to reuse should be built with the count as an input, and you have to ask for that.

Historical: on 4 September the app and the website showed different prices. On first login the app opened a '7-days free trial' panel listing Basic at $16, Essential at $70 and Advanced at $120 a month, with $20, $100 and $200 struck through, while the public pricing page, read the day before, still charged $20, $100 and $200 monthly. That gap closed by 13 September: the public page now shows the same $16, $70 and $120.

What this test does not show. books.toscrape.com is a static sandbox with no login, no JavaScript rendering and no anti-bot measures, so none of the managed-browser, proxy or CAPTCHA infrastructure in BrowserAct's pitch was exercised. It proves the no-code loop from plain prompt to reusable Bot; it says nothing about hostile sites, where proxy use starts to matter -- free in the cloud for a limited time, 5,000 credits per gigabyte of dynamic proxy traffic on the Local CLI.
